vignette:
Nikhil Patel, a 46-year-old non-binary software engineer, came to treatment after more than a year of living as if danger could break through ordinary moments without warning. The trauma they returned to in fragments began after a minor street confrontation on their bike commute home. A police officer had stopped them after a driver complained that Nikhil had “cut into traffic.” What began as a tense exchange escalated quickly when Nikhil, already upset, questioned why they were being singled out. The officer moved closer, shouted over them, and forced them to the ground. Nikhil remembered the shock of pavement against their cheek, the pressure of a knee pinning them, the exposure of strangers looking on, and the officer’s certainty that any resistance meant threat. Their spouse later pieced together much of what happened from Nikhil’s account and a bystander video, because Nikhil themselves could not hold the episode as one continuous story.

In the weeks after, the reminders that cut deepest were oddly inconsistent to anyone else but made immediate sense to Nikhil. Seeing other people cycling in the city could pull them straight back into the stop, not as a full recollection but as a wave of dread and humiliation in their body. With that jolt came the thought, immediate and convincing, that ordinary public life could turn dangerous without warning and that they could be singled out and overpowered again at any time. In those moments, the conclusion landed with it: if something as ordinary as a bike lane could turn into danger, then nowhere in the city was governed by rules they could trust, and other people could at any moment decide to overpower or expose them. Confrontations at work—an irritated product manager raising their voice in a meeting, a disagreement in a code review—made their chest tighten and their attention lock onto exits and barriers. Even feeling relaxed with their spouse on a good evening could suddenly become dangerous; the moment they noticed themselves softening or laughing, they would tense, as if calm itself left them unprotected. These moments did not just unsettle them. They brought with them a sense that the world no longer followed any reliable rules, that harm could come from anywhere and anyone, and that other people could somehow see what had been done to them.

Nikhil spoke about the event in starts and stops. They would begin describing the stop on the street, get as far as the officer’s hand on their shoulder or the sound of a voice ordering them down, and then mentally shut the door before the memory could fully form. At other times there was no picture at all, only the full force of terror and shame arriving in their body without warning. Because they could not assemble a clear narrative even for themselves, the memory remained unfinished and strangely alive; when something reminded them of the assault, it was not experienced as a past event but as a felt emergency. After one of these memory surges, the world seemed to fill with matching pieces: voices sounded sharper, strangers seemed to stand too close, and the bikes moving through traffic below the office windows began to register as if the memory itself were teaching them what to notice. And after one of those memory surges, they began to find pieces of the assault everywhere, as if the memory itself taught their attention what to seize on next: the angle of a stranger stepping too close, the bark of an order, the sight of bikes moving through traffic below the office windows. That made them even more watchful in the present. On the train to work they chose seats with a wall at their back and a clear view of the car. In the office they tracked coworkers’ movements and tone for signs that someone might turn aggressive. Living with that constant sense of imminent danger became, for Nikhil, its own proof that the assault had permanently changed what kind of world this was and what kind of person they now were—someone marked, exposed, and unlikely ever to be fully safe again. Feeling under threat so much of the time persuaded them that their fear was not excessive but accurate, confirming the belief that safety was no longer something available to them in the way it seemed to be for other people.

Over time, what Nikhil concluded about the assault tightened around these reactions. They had come to believe that whatever assumptions they once had about fairness, professionalism, or basic safety had been shattered. Once they were living by that conclusion, more and more ordinary moments started to catch on it: a cyclist waiting at a light, a clipped tone in a meeting, even a relaxed evening at home could flare into reminders because their mind was already treating the world as a place where danger hid inside normality. Once they were living by that belief, ordinary cues snagged much more easily; a cyclist at an intersection, a sharp voice in the office, even the feeling of relaxing with their spouse could register immediately as warnings rather than neutral moments. The officer had looked ordinary until he was not; from this, Nikhil became certain that you can never know who will harm you. They also felt marked by the experience, as if the violation was visible on them and other people could read it in their face or posture. Those beliefs made it harder to stay with the memory long enough to make sense of it. Each time an image or bodily surge began, they pushed it away before it could complete, partly because to remember fully felt like becoming exposed again.

Their daily life narrowed around anticipation of threat. At the software company where they worked hybrid, they avoided in-person meetings when possible and, when attendance was unavoidable, arrived early to secure the seat they deemed safest—never boxed in, always near a door. In tense conversations they watched others closely, trying to detect who might humiliate or corner them. That constant scanning only confirmed to them that danger was everywhere; every raised voice, every abrupt gesture, every cyclist passing the conference-room windows on the street below became another sign that the world was fundamentally unsafe. Already keyed up, they found that almost anything could tip into a reminder, as though the background hum of danger itself was turning neutral details into warnings they could not afford to ignore. The more they lived in that state, the more readily ordinary cues triggered them. A happy, unguarded Saturday morning could flip into vigilance simply because they noticed themselves feeling peaceful and then thought how quickly peace had once been taken away.

By the time Nikhil sought help, their spouse was pleading with them to stop arranging every outing around escape routes and to stop leaving restaurants whenever a nearby table became loud or argumentative. Nikhil was exhausted by how often their body reacted before they understood why, and by how little of the original event they could bear to know. What frightened them most was the sense that the assault had not ended but had scattered into the world, waiting in cyclists, in conflict, in moments of ease, in other people’s faces. What they hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget, but to be able to sit through a meeting or a quiet evening at home without feeling that harm was already on its way.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that reminders or cues directly lead Nikhil to negative beliefs or appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that Nikhil’s negative beliefs themselves make cues or reminders more likely to be noticed or experienced as triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that the trauma memory directly generates or amplifies triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly state in one paragraph that Nikhil’s sense of threat leads to or strengthens negative beliefs/appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
